    • US Economics Weekly Update

    US Economics Weekly Update 10/1/2026

    Research | Economics | 1 October 2026 | 10:15PM UTC

    We forecast that payrolls rose 80k (vs. 88k consensus) and the unemployment rate fell to 4.0% (vs. 4.1% consensus) in September.

    • Layoffs remains low and big data indicators of job growth rose, but September payroll growth has underperformed its trend when Labor Day is later in the month, like this year.

    • The recent decline in continuing claims points to a small decline in the unemployment rate.

    • We forecast 0.2% (vs. 0.3% consensus) average hourly earnings growth, reflecting negative calendar effects.  Our wage tracker stands at 3.5% year-over-year.

    We pushed back our forecast for the next Fed hike to December.

    • Following better inflation news (below), NY Fed President Williams’ comment that “there is no need for urgency,” and Vice Chair Jefferson’s comment that “any future adjustments in policy should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data,” the FOMC now appears likely to pause in October.

    • We expect a second and final hike in December but see a strong chance that the FOMC will ultimately conclude that additional rate hikes are unnecessary.

    • We remain skeptical of the economic case for raising rates.  We see little sign of overheating and estimate that tariffs and the Iran war account for 0.9pp of core PCE inflation’s 1pp overshoot of 2%.

    Methodological changes lowered year-over-year core PCE inflation more than expected to 3.0%.

    • The revisions lowered the year-over-year rate by 0.36pp, with most of that coming from portfolio management (-0.23pp) and computer accessories and software (-0.11pp).

    • August core PCE inflation also came in a bit softer than expected at 0.25%.

    • Following the revisions, core PCE inflation averaged 0.17% over the last 3 months or 2.0% annualized.

    We expect core PCE inflation of 23bp in September and October and 16bp in November and December.

    • Two factors will boost the next two months:

      • Energy price passthrough is likely to likely to boost airfares by 3% in September and contribute 3-5bp to the core overall for the next few months.

      • Distortions to the October seasonal factors caused by missing data from last year’s government shutdown should boost October core CPI inflation by 5bp and core PCE inflation by a bit less.

    • After that, we expect the trend to fall, in part because shelter inflation should remain cool.

    Core inflation should substantially undershoot the FOMC’s forecast.

    • We now expect core PCE inflation to stand at 3.0% year-over-year in 2026 Q4, 0.4pp below the 3.4% median FOMC forecast from the September meeting.

    Our 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth forecast rose to 2.5% following upward revisions to Q1 and Q2.

    • Q1 GDP growth was revised up 0.4pp to +2.5%, and Q2 GDP growth was revised up 0.7pp to +2.2%.

    • Our Q3 GDP growth estimate stands at 3.4% following strong construction spending, 0.6% real consumption growth, a widening in the trade deficit, and a rise in new home sales in August.

    Research recap: Why has the US economy been so resilient to higher rates and higher oil prices?

    • Our financial conditions index framework implies that the economic impact of higher rates has been partially offset by the effects of higher equity prices and narrower credit spreads.

    • Higher oil and refined product prices weigh on real income and consumer spending, though the net impact on GDP has more recently been partially offset by the increase in US energy capex.

    • The most surprising part of US economic performance this year is the impressive 3.9% annualized growth pace of real consumer spending from February to August despite higher energy prices.

    The saving rate was revised up and now stands at 4.1%.

    • The upward revision came largely from an upward revision to interest income, which we previously noted was understated, contributing to an understatement of the saving rate and GDI.

    David MericleGoldman Sachs & Co. LLC, New Yorkdavid.mericle@gs.com
